content.content:
A draft's jj workspace is created under one per-user draft-workspace root that lies outside the repository, at a path inside that root derived from the record's handle. The root is one for the user, not one for the repository; the path is the repository's own namespace under that root together with the handle of the record the draft is held for. Location, ownership and derivation are one answer to one question — where a draft's working copy lives — because each holds the other two up: a root inside the repository could not hold copies of the repository's tree, a root belonging to the repository could not be reached from outside it, and a path not derived from the handle would have to be chosen per draft, which is a second owner of the same answer.

The workspace goes outside the repository because a workspace is a working copy of the repository's tree, while the repository root is itself already a working copy — the state directory the registry lives in is a directory of the repository (ulqqklzk). The registry's place is the mirror of this, not a rival to it: the record lives in one registry under `.deccy/work/` because it is deccy's state and untracked, so nothing the repository tracks contains it or has to contain it (ulqqklzk). A record carries the workspace as one of its references — it points at the workspace rather than holding it (owyntkvw) — so the workspace is not part of the registry, and the registry's place says nothing about where the working copy goes. A working copy is the opposite kind of thing — a checkout of the repository's own content — so it cannot take the place the record takes: under `.deccy/` it would be one checkout of the tree nested inside the tree. The two locations are the two sides of the distinction that node draws, and neither moves to the other's place without ceasing to be what it is.

The root belongs to the user because the workspace's home is nowhere the repository can name. The only place inside the repository that deccy keeps for its own state is the state directory, and what lives there is the record, not the working copy (ulqqklzk). A record states where a draft's workspace is by naming it, and a name is a reference, not a place to search from (owyntkvw); because the workspace is outside the repository, the path a record names cannot be stated relative to the repository, and nothing in the repository can be consulted to derive it. One root that exists for the user on that machine, outside every repository, is what makes the answer the same for every repository: the drafts of two repositories written by one user sit under one root, each in the repository's own namespace, and neither repository gains a directory it does not own.

The path is derived from the handle because the handle is the only thing that picks out one draft (owyntkvw). A record's identity is its handle, and its node and edit are references: one node may be named by several records at once — competing alternatives within one edit, or a redraft while an earlier draft is still open — and one edit is named by the records of every node it touches. A path keyed by node or by edit would therefore put two drafts at one directory, which is exactly what the draft model forbids: each draft is written in its own workspace, so the drafts of one edit can be written in parallel (znskspqs). The handle is one per draft, so a path derived from it is one per draft: distinct drafts get distinct directories, the derivation is evaluated without consulting any other draft, and two drafts can be opened at the same time without an agreement between them. Because handles are minted inside one registry, the repository's namespace under the root keeps that property across repositories: a handle names a directory within its own registry's namespace only.

Deriving the path does not take the reference out of the record. A record still names the workspace that holds its draft by name and path, and that naming remains a reference and not custody (owyntkvw): the derivation fixes what the reference says when the record is written, so that the record and any reader holding the handle agree on one directory, while the registry stays the only place the draft's workspace is stated. What the derivation fixes is the value of that reference, not its standing: the path names a part of the draft, not the record, and the record's key remains the handle. Nothing here creates a workspace, removes one, names its jj name, or decides what a missing workspace means; those belong to the commitments that own them.

These clauses are one commitment. The root being outside the repository is what lets it hold working copies; the root being per-user is what makes it reachable from outside every repository; and the derivation from the handle is what keeps one root from putting two drafts in one directory. Change the first and the workspace sits inside the tree it copies, change the second and the path cannot be found without the repository, change the third and drafts collide. They answer one question — where a draft's working copy lives — with one answer: under the user's own root, outside the repository, at the directory the record's handle names.
content.rationale:
The draft's working copy needs a home that no repository owns. Each draft is written in its own workspace and the drafts of one edit are written in parallel (znskspqs), so a draft's workspace must exist as a directory distinct from the trunk's working copy and from every other draft's; the trunk's working copy holds the repository root, so another checkout of that tree cannot be placed inside it. The path must also be known from the record alone: a record's identity is its handle, and its node and edit are references that are many per record — one node may be named by several records at once (owyntkvw) — so the only thing that picks out one draft is the handle. Deriving the directory from the handle is therefore the one derivation that gives every draft its own path and lets two drafts be opened at once with no naming step between them. Because handles are minted inside one registry, the per-user root carries the repository's namespace, so that the same property survives across repositories written by one user on one machine.

The state side stays where its own node put it. The record lives in the one registry under `.deccy/work/` inside the state directory, untracked with it, because what the registry holds is deccy's state and not repository content (ulqqklzk). That is precisely why the workspace cannot follow it: a working copy is a checkout of the repository's own content, so the argument that gives the registry its untracked home has no application to it, and placing it under `.deccy/` would put a checkout of the tree inside the tree. The two places are the two sides of one distinction; moving the workspace into the state directory would contradict ulqqklzk's reason for the registry's place, not extend it.

The record keeps its reference. A record names the workspace that holds its draft by name and path (owyntkvw); the derivation fixes the path the record states but does not replace that field, so a reader holding the handle and the record arrives at the directory the draft was written in. Nothing here creates or removes a workspace, decides what a missing one means, names the jj workspace, or fixes the verb that opens a draft; the surface above this node decides those, and this node remains the answer to where the working copy lives.
